rw: A CD locks in a fixed rate for a set term, which usually beats a regular savings rate, so it suits money you will not need until the term ends.

ww.CDs have no interest and are less safe t: Certificates of deposit do pay interest, usually more than regular savings, and they are FDIC insured up to limits, so this claim is false.
ww.CDs allow unlimited withdrawals at any t: Unlimited penalty-free withdrawals describe a regular savings or checking account; a CD locks money until maturity and charges a penalty for early withdrawal.
ww.CDs are not insured and can be lost in f: CDs from banks are covered by FDIC insurance (or NCUA at credit unions) up to $250,000 per depositor, so a bank failure does not wipe them out.

rw: Direct deposit has an employer send part of each paycheck straight into savings, which builds the habit of paying yourself first without relying on willpower.

ww.Buying a gift card for a friend at a loc: A gift card is a purchase made at a store; it has nothing to do with sending part of your paycheck into a savings account.
ww.Paying cash to a cashier at the register: Paying cash at a register is a spending transaction at a store, not a way of moving earnings into savings.
ww.Writing a check each month to the saving: Writing a monthly check is a manual deposit you must remember each time; direct deposit is automatic and requires no check.

rw: Gain = 10 shares x ($32 - $25) = 10 x $7 = $70, the difference between the sale price and the purchase price before fees and taxes.

ww.$250: $250 is the original purchase cost of 10 shares at $25 each; it is what she paid, not the profit she made.
ww.$7: $7 is the gain on a single share; she owns 10 shares, so the total gain must be multiplied by 10.
ww.$320: $320 is the total sale proceeds (10 x $32), not the gain; the gain subtracts the $250 she originally paid.

rw: U.S. Treasury securities are backed by the full faith and credit of the federal government, so default risk is extremely low compared with other investments.

ww.A single speculative stock: A single speculative stock can swing sharply or lose most of its value, so it carries far more risk than government-backed securities.
ww.A start-up investment: Start-up investments often fail, and investors can lose everything, which makes them one of the riskiest places to put money.
ww.A new cryptocurrency: A new cryptocurrency is highly volatile and mostly unregulated with no guarantee behind it, so it is among the riskiest investments available.

rw: Employee contributes 6% x $50,000 = $3,000, and the employer matches 50% of it: 0.50 x $3,000 = $1,500 of free retirement money.

ww.$750: $750 would be a 25% match on the $3,000 contribution; the plan matches 50 cents per dollar, which is double this amount.
ww.$6,000: $6,000 is twelve percent of pay; the match is capped at 6% of $50,000 and paid at only 50 cents on the dollar.
ww.$3,000: $3,000 is the employee's own contribution (6% x $50,000); a 50% match pays half of that, not the full amount.

rw: With 40 years until retirement, a young investor has time to recover from market declines and benefit from long-term growth, so she can accept more risk.

ww.Older people never invest in the stock m: Many older investors do hold stocks, often alongside bonds, so saying they never invest in the market is simply false and unrelated to risk capacity.
ww.Younger people cannot lose money in the: Young investors can certainly lose money, since stock prices fall at any age; they simply have more time to recover before needing the money.
ww.Retirement accounts are always fully ins: Retirement accounts are not insured against market losses; FDIC insurance covers bank deposits, not stocks or funds held inside an IRA or 401(k).

rw: Spreading money across different investments means one poor performer hurts less, so diversification reduces the impact of any single investment's decline.

ww.It means owning only one stock to focus: Owning only one stock is the opposite of diversification and leaves the whole portfolio exposed to a single company's fortunes.
ww.It eliminates all risk from the portfoli: Diversification lowers risk but cannot eliminate it, since market-wide events can hurt nearly all investments at the same time.
ww.It guarantees profits on every investmen: No strategy guarantees profits, and diversification only spreads risk; investments can still lose value even when held for a year or longer.

rw: A capital gain is the profit made when you sell an asset, such as a stock or home, for more than you paid for it.

ww.A tax refund that the state pays to a wo: A tax refund is money returned by the government when too much tax was withheld; it is not a profit from selling an investment.
ww.A bank fee charged when your account bal: A low-balance charge is an account fee, a cost to the customer, while a capital gain is a profit earned on an investment.
ww.A regular paycheck from an employer for: A paycheck is wage income earned from working, while a capital gain comes from an asset such as a stock rising in value.

rw: Short-term prices can drop, and if you need the money in six months you may be forced to sell at a loss with no time to wait for recovery.

ww.Stocks cannot be sold at any time or at: Stocks trade on exchanges and can usually be sold on any market day, so liquidity is not the problem; the risk is the price you might get.
ww.Stocks always rise in six months, so the: Stocks never always rise over short periods, and a six-month window has no guaranteed gain, so this claim is false.
ww.Stocks pay no returns to those who buy a: Stocks can pay returns through dividends and price growth; the short-term risk is about price swings, not about earning nothing.

rw: A financial adviser gives guidance on saving, investing, insurance, and retirement so clients can make informed decisions about their money.

ww.Guarantees returns on all of your invest: No adviser can guarantee investment returns, and promising guaranteed gains is a warning sign of fraud rather than a duty of a legitimate adviser.
ww.Collects taxes from clients on the money: Collecting taxes is the job of government agencies such as the IRS; an adviser may help with tax planning but does not collect taxes.
ww.Sets interest rates for the banks of a w: Interest rates for a nation are set by its central bank, such as the Federal Reserve in the U.S., not by a financial adviser.

rw: After a 50% loss, $100 becomes $50, and doubling $50 back to $100 requires a 100% gain, because percent gains apply to the smaller base.

ww.25%: A 25% gain on $50 yields only $62.50, still well short of the original $100 value.
ww.75%: A 75% gain on $50 yields $87.50, which is still below the original $100, so it is not enough to break even.
ww.50.0%: A 50% gain on $50 gives only $75, so the investor would remain $25 short of the original $100 value.

rw: An expense ratio is the annual percentage of fund assets charged to cover management and operating costs, which lowers the investor's return each year.

ww.A tax refund paid to investors each year: A tax refund is a payment from the government; an expense ratio is a charge investors pay, and it reduces their returns.
ww.A free service offered to fund investors: Funds are not free; management, administration, and trading costs are real and are passed on to investors through the expense ratio.
ww.A bonus paid to investors who hold a fun: Fees are costs, not rewards; investors pay them, and they are never a bonus for holding a fund.

rw: A portfolio is the full collection of investments, such as stocks, bonds, and funds, held by an individual, family, or institution.

ww.A savings account that pays a fixed rate: A savings account that pays a fixed rate is a single deposit product; a portfolio is a whole collection of different holdings.
ww.A paycheck that an employer gives to a w: A paycheck is income from an employer for work done, not a set of investments that a person owns.
ww.A bank statement listing deposits and wi: A bank statement lists deposits and withdrawals for an account; it records transactions, not the mix of investments someone owns.

rw: No real investment can guarantee high returns without risk; this promise is the classic sign of a Ponzi scheme or other investment fraud.

ww.Registered advisers with a clean public: Registered advisers with a clean public record are a good sign; you can check an adviser's background through regulators such as FINRA or the SEC.
ww.A clear explanation of the risks and pas: Honest sellers explain risks and show past results clearly, so a clear explanation is a sign of a legitimate offer, not a scam.
ww.Written disclosures of fees, risks and p: Written disclosures of fees, risks, and results are required for legitimate investments and signal transparency rather than fraud.

rw: Rule of 72: years to double = 72 divided by the rate, so 72 / 6 = 12 years for money to double at a 6% annual return.

ww.6 years: Six years simply repeats the interest rate; dividing 72 by 6 gives 12 years, not 6.
ww.1 year: One year would require a 72% return to double, far above the 6% rate stated in this problem.
ww.72 years: Seventy-two is the numerator in the rule, not the answer; you must divide it by the 6% rate to get 12 years.

rw: Utilization = balance / limit = $1,000 / $2,000 = 50%, which is high; keeping it under 30% is better for a credit score.

ww.100%: A 100% utilization would require a $2,000 balance on a $2,000 limit, which is double the balance she actually carries.
ww.20%: Twenty percent would need a $400 balance on a $2,000 limit; her balance is $1,000, so utilization is higher than that.
ww.200%: A 200% utilization would mean owing $4,000 on a $2,000 limit; her $1,000 balance is only half of the limit.

rw: Lenders review credit history, income, and existing debts to judge how likely a borrower is to repay the loan on time.

ww.Shoe size and hair color too: Physical traits like shoe size and hair color have no bearing on whether a borrower can repay, and lenders may not use them to decide.
ww.Social media followers and likes: Social media popularity says nothing about repayment ability, so lenders do not weigh followers or likes in a loan decision.
ww.Favorite color of the applicant: A favorite color has no connection to the ability to repay, so it plays no role in a lender's decision.

rw: With identical terms, a lower APR means less total interest paid, so the 4% APR loan is the cheaper option.

ww.Neither costs: Loans always cost something, since interest is the price of borrowing; 'neither costs' ignores that both loans charge interest.
ww.The 6% APR loan: A 6% APR charges more interest per year than 4% on identical terms, so the 6% loan is the more expensive choice.
ww.They cost the same: The rates differ by two percentage points, so the costs differ; the 6% loan charges noticeably more interest over the same term.

rw: A secured card is backed by a cash deposit, which lowers the lender's risk and makes approval easier for people building credit for the first time.

ww.A big home mortgage loan: A mortgage needs good credit and a large down payment, so someone with no credit history is unlikely to qualify for one first.
ww.A small business loan: Business loans typically require financial records, collateral, or a track record, which a person with no credit history lacks.
ww.A large unsecured limit: Large unsecured limits go to borrowers with proven credit; with no history, lenders will not offer a big limit without collateral.

rw: A hard inquiry happens when a lender reviews your credit report because you applied for credit, and it can lower your score slightly for a while.

ww.You closed an account and the bank check: Closing an account does not create an inquiry; a hard inquiry occurs when a lender pulls your report in response to an application.
ww.You paid a bill early and the lender tha: Paying a bill early may help your record, but it does not trigger a hard inquiry; those come from credit applications.
ww.You checked your own score and no lender: Checking your own score is a soft inquiry that does not affect your score, which is the opposite of a hard inquiry.

rw: A grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the statement balance in full by the due date, usually about 21 days.

ww.A permanent waiver of fees on every purc: A grace period does not waive fees permanently; fees such as annual or late fees still apply when they are charged.
ww.A reward for late payment that the issue: Late payments are penalized, not rewarded; a grace period only applies when the full balance is paid by the due date.
ww.The time to ignore the bill without any: The grace period does not allow ignoring the bill; unpaid balances start accruing interest, and late payments bring fees and credit damage.

rw: At 20% APR on $3,000 (about $600 a year), minimum payments mostly cover interest, so the balance shrinks slowly and the debt lasts for years.

ww.Interest stops being charged and the who: Interest keeps accruing on the unpaid balance, so paying only the minimum never wipes out the debt or stops charges.
ww.The credit limit is cut to zero, so the: Issuers do not cut a limit to zero for paying the minimum; the real problem is that interest keeps compounding on the remaining balance.
ww.The debt is erased quickly and the card: Minimum payments pay down debt slowly, not quickly, and the bank does not close an account simply because minimums are made.

rw: Errors such as wrong balances or accounts that are not yours can lower your score and lead to higher rates or denied credit.

ww.Credit reports are private and cannot be: Credit reports can be corrected; under the Fair Credit Reporting Act you can dispute errors with the bureaus and the lender.
ww.Reports never contain errors of any kind: Reports do contain mistakes, and studies have found errors on many of them, which is why free annual checks are recommended.
ww.Errors only help you and never cost you: Errors usually hurt, not help; wrong late payments or accounts can raise your borrowing costs, so checking is worthwhile.

rw: A 29% APR is very high, so comparing lower-rate options and paying the full balance monthly avoids costly interest charges.

ww.Carry a balance to build credit, as lend: Carrying a balance does not build credit; it only racks up interest at 29%, and paying on time and in full is what lenders reward.
ww.Ignore the APR and sign up for the card: Ignoring the APR is risky because the rate determines the cost of carrying a balance, and 29% is much higher than typical cards.
ww.Take every offer that arrives in the mai: Accepting every mailed offer can create many accounts and hard inquiries and tempt overspending, which can hurt a young person's finances.

rw: $45 / $300 = 15% per two weeks; with 26 two-week periods in a year, 15% x 26 = 390% APR, which is why payday loans are so costly.

ww.About 15.0%: About 15% is the fee as a share of the loan for one two-week period ($45 / $300), not the annualized rate.
ww.About 45%: 45% mistakes the $45 fee for a percentage; the fee is 15% of $300 and must be annualized to get the APR.
ww.About 0%: The loan charges a $45 fee, so the APR cannot be zero; the fee on $300 works out to a very high annual rate.

rw: Default means failing to make required payments, which can bring late fees, collections, credit damage, and possibly loss of collateral.

ww.To refinance the loan at a lower rate: Refinancing replaces a loan with a new one at better terms; it is a deliberate action, not a failure to pay.
ww.To pay the loan off early in full: Paying off a loan early in full is a good outcome that closes the debt; it is the opposite of defaulting.
ww.To ask a question about your loan: Asking a question about a loan is normal customer service and has no effect on the loan or your payment record.

rw: Refinancing replaces an existing loan with a new loan, often to get a lower rate, lower payment, or different term.

ww.Paying a loan with a credit card, moving: Paying a loan with a credit card just moves the debt to a different lender and is not what refinancing means; refinancing replaces the loan itself.
ww.Ignoring a loan and not paying it back t: Ignoring a loan is a default, which damages credit and can lead to collections; refinancing is a planned change of terms.
ww.Canceling insurance that you pay for eve: Canceling insurance is unrelated to loans; refinancing deals with replacing existing debt, not coverage payments.

rw: Payment history and utilization are the biggest score factors, so paying bills on time and keeping balances low builds good credit over time.

ww.Max out your cards each month for fun: Maxing out cards drives utilization up, which hurts your score and creates large debts that cost interest.
ww.Close all accounts that you have opened: Closing accounts shortens your credit history and cuts available credit, which can raise utilization and lower your score.
ww.Apply for many cards at once to get cred: Applying for many cards at once creates multiple hard inquiries and signals risk, which can lower your score.

rw: A credit card is a loan you repay later, often with interest, while a debit card pulls money straight from your own account.

ww.They are identical in every way and in e: Credit and debit cards work differently: credit borrows from the issuer, while debit takes money directly from your checking account.
ww.Debit cards charge interest monthly on t: Debit cards use your own funds and do not charge interest, so describing them as charging interest monthly is wrong.
ww.Credit cards use only your cash and neve: Credit cards lend you money up to a limit, so saying they use only your cash and no loan describes debit cards instead.

rw: Planning to pay off the balance before the 0% period ends avoids the 22% rate, so she gets the benefit of the offer without the cost.

ww.Spend as much as possible in the promoti: After 12 months the rate jumps to 22%, so heavy spending without a payoff plan could leave a large balance charged that high rate.
ww.Ignore the end date of the offer and kee: Ignoring the end date risks owing a big balance at 22% APR, which can erase any benefit of the promotion.
ww.Make no payments until the offer ends in: Not paying anything for a year wastes the 0% window, and late payments or missing minimums can cancel the promotional rate.

rw: Utilization = balances divided by total credit limits, and keeping it low, ideally below 30%, helps your credit score.

ww.The fee for a card that you pay each yea: An annual fee is a yearly charge for holding the card, while utilization compares your balance to your credit limit.
ww.The number of cards you own on the credi: The number of cards you own is a different credit factor; utilization measures how much of your available limit you are using.
ww.The interest on a card that is charged m: Monthly interest is a cost of carrying a balance; the utilization ratio is a percentage of credit used, not a charge.

rw: Insurer pays covered cost minus the deductible: $4,000 - $1,000 = $3,000, while the driver pays the $1,000 deductible.

ww.$5,000: $5,000 adds the deductible to the repair cost; insurance pays the covered cost minus the deductible, so it cannot exceed the bill.
ww.$4,000: The insurer does not pay the full $4,000 because the policyholder pays the first $1,000 deductible out of pocket.
ww.$1,000: $1,000 is the deductible, which the driver pays, not the amount the insurer pays.

rw: Collision coverage pays to repair or replace your own car after a crash with another vehicle or object, regardless of who was at fault.

ww.Life insurance: Life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries and has nothing to do with repairing your car after an accident.
ww.Health insurance: Health insurance covers medical expenses for illness or injury, not damage to a vehicle.
ww.Renters insurance plan: Renters insurance covers belongings and liability in a rented home, not damage to your car in an accident.

rw: Renters insurance covers a tenant's personal property against theft, fire, and other covered events, and often includes liability coverage as well.

ww.Disability insurance: Disability insurance replaces income if you cannot work due to injury or illness; it does not cover stolen or burned possessions.
ww.Auto insurance: Auto insurance protects a vehicle and driver liability, and a renter's household belongings inside the apartment are not covered by it.
ww.Term life insurance: Term life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries, not the replacement cost of belongings lost to theft or fire.

rw: Term life pays a death benefit to beneficiaries if the insured dies during a set term, such as 10, 20, or 30 years.

ww.Coverage for car damage and its repairs: Coverage for car damage and repairs is provided by auto insurance, not by a life insurance policy of any kind.
ww.Income during retirement paid out each m: Retirement income comes from annuities, pensions, or Social Security; term life insurance pays only when the insured person dies.
ww.Lifetime investment growth with a cash v: Cash value and lifetime coverage belong to permanent policies such as whole life; term insurance has no cash value.

rw: Health insurance pays part of medical costs, with the insured sharing costs through premiums, deductibles, and copays.

ww.Paying property taxes owed: Property taxes are paid to local government and are not covered by health insurance, which handles medical expenses.
ww.Paying for groceries each week: Groceries are everyday living costs; health insurance only helps pay medical bills such as doctor visits and hospital stays.
ww.Paying all costs, no deductible: Health insurance rarely pays everything; deductibles, copays, and coinsurance mean the insured still pays a share of costs.

rw: A higher deductible means you carry more of each loss, so the insurer charges a lower premium in return.

ww.More coverage added: Adding coverage increases what the insurer might pay out, so it normally raises the premium rather than lowering it.
ww.A lower deductible: A lower deductible shifts more cost to the insurer, which typically raises the premium rather than lowering it.
ww.More claims filed: Filing more claims marks a driver as higher risk, which tends to raise premiums at renewal rather than lower them.

rw: Strong, unique passwords plus regular monitoring of accounts and credit reports help prevent and quickly catch identity theft.

ww.Ignore bank statements when they arrive: Ignoring bank statements lets fraud go unnoticed; reviewing statements is how you catch unauthorized charges early.
ww.Share your passwords with friends and wi: Sharing passwords gives others access to your accounts and raises the chance of theft or misuse, even with trusted people.
ww.Use one simple password everywhere, so i: One simple password reused everywhere means a single breach exposes every account, so reuse is a major security weakness.

rw: Contact the company through a number or app you already trust; unexpected texts like this are typical phishing attempts.

ww.Reply with your card number and your PIN: Sending a card number and PIN to someone who texted you hands criminals what they need to commit fraud.
ww.Forward it to friends and ask what they: Forwarding a phishing message may spread it to others and does nothing to verify whether your account is really locked.
ww.Click the link and enter your password b: Clicking the link and entering a password sends your login to scammers, who built the urgency to rush you into acting.

rw: Liability insurance pays for injury or property damage you cause to others, and covers legal defense costs if you are sued.

ww.Coverage for your own injuries only, non: Covering only your own injuries describes other policies; liability insurance protects others harmed by your actions.
ww.A warranty on a product that you have re: A warranty covers repair or replacement of a defective product, while liability insurance covers harm you cause to others.
ww.A savings account for lawsuits that a fi: Insurance is a risk-sharing contract with an insurer, not a savings account that a firm sets aside for lawsuits.

rw: Self-insuring means setting aside your own money, such as an emergency fund, to pay for small, predictable losses instead of buying insurance.

ww.Ignoring risk completely and hoping noth: Ignoring a risk hoping nothing goes wrong is not self-insuring because there is no plan or funds set aside for a loss.
ww.Borrowing at high interest to pay for ev: Borrowing at high interest after each loss is costly and unplanned, unlike self-insuring, which relies on money saved beforehand.
ww.Buying a full policy for every risk, how: Buying a policy for every small risk transfers risk to an insurer, which is the opposite of self-insuring.

rw: Avoiding a risk means not doing the activity that creates it, such as not riding a motorcycle to avoid the chance of a crash.

ww.Accept it and plan to pay for any loss y: Accepting a risk and planning to pay for any loss yourself is risk retention, not risk avoidance.
ww.Reduce its effects with safety steps and: Using safety steps and training is risk reduction, which lowers the chance or size of a loss instead of eliminating the activity.
ww.Buy a policy for it, so an insurer pays: Buying insurance transfers the financial risk to an insurer, which is risk transfer rather than avoidance.

rw: Bodily injury liability pays medical costs and related claims for people you injure when you are at fault in an accident.

ww.Roadside assistance plan: Roadside assistance covers towing, jump-starts, and similar services for your own car, not medical bills of an injured person.
ww.Comprehensive insurance: Comprehensive insurance covers non-collision damage to your own car, such as theft, fire, hail, or hitting an animal.
ww.Collision coverage plan: Collision coverage pays for damage to your own vehicle, and it does not pay medical bills for another person you injured.

rw: Bookstore total is $12 + $1.50 = $13.50 per hour, which is less than the café's $15, so the café pays $1.50 more per hour.

ww.The bookstore at $13.50, because tips ar: The bookstore pays $12 + $1.50 = $13.50 per hour, but that is less than the café's $15, and tips are not always higher.
ww.They pay exactly the same per hour of wo: The totals differ: the café pays $15 per hour while the bookstore averages $13.50, so the two jobs do not pay the same.
ww.The bookstore at $12 plus extra benefits: Even if benefits were counted, the question asks about pay per hour, and the bookstore's $13.50 is already below the café's $15.

rw: A W-2 is issued by an employer after year end and shows total wages and taxes withheld for the full year.

ww.A W-4 form: A W-4 is filled out by the employee to tell the employer how much tax to withhold; it does not report annual earnings.
ww.A pay stub: A pay stub shows earnings and deductions for a single pay period, not the totals for the entire year.
ww.A bank record: A bank record lists deposits and withdrawals, but it does not show gross earnings and taxes withheld the way a W-2 does.

rw: Employers withhold income tax so employees pay part of their tax bill gradually during the year instead of in one lump sum.

ww.To pay the company's profits out to the: Withholding is taken from employee wages and sent to the government, not used to pay company profits to the owners.
ww.To lower the employee's wage rate, so th: Withholding does not change the wage rate; it simply sends part of the employee's earned pay to the tax authorities.
ww.To fund the employee's vacation and sick: Vacation and sick days are employer benefits; withheld income tax goes to the government and not to those benefits.

rw: Biweekly means 26 pay periods a year, so gross pay per check is $52,000 / 26 = $2,000 before taxes and deductions.

ww.$1,000: $1,000 is the weekly amount ($52,000 / 52), but biweekly pay comes every two weeks, so each check is double that.
ww.$4,333: $4,333 is the monthly figure ($52,000 / 12), which does not match a biweekly pay schedule.
ww.$26,000: $26,000 is half a year's pay ($52,000 / 2), as if paid twice a year, not every two weeks.

rw: A signing bonus is a one-time payment an employer offers to attract a new hire, often with conditions such as staying a certain time.

ww.A fee for starting work, paid by the new: A signing bonus is paid by the employer to the new hire, not a fee the new hire pays to start working.
ww.A yearly tax refund from the state or ci: A tax refund comes from the government after filing a return, whereas a signing bonus is paid by an employer.
ww.A monthly loan paid back to the employer: A signing bonus is a payment to the worker, not a loan to be repaid monthly to the employer.

rw: Employers promote workers who consistently perform well and keep building new skills, since those workers show reliability and growth potential.

ww.Doing the minimum amount of work that is: Doing only the minimum rarely shows initiative, and managers usually promote employees who go beyond basic expectations.
ww.Arguing with supervisors about every dec: Arguing with supervisors about every decision damages working relationships and makes promotion less likely.
ww.Avoiding responsibility for any of the t: Avoiding responsibility shows a lack of reliability, so employers are unlikely to trust such a worker with a higher position.

rw: The match is 6% x $45,000 = $2,700 per year of extra compensation that Offer B does not provide to the worker.

ww.$27,000: $27,000 is ten times the correct amount; 6% of $45,000 is $2,700, not 60%.
ww.$0: Offer A provides a match and Offer B does not, so the difference cannot be zero when she contributes 6%.
ww.$270: $270 would be 0.6% of salary, a decimal slip; 6% of $45,000 is $2,700.

rw: A union is an organization of workers that bargains collectively with employers over pay, benefits, and working conditions.

ww.A government tax office that collects in: The tax office is a government agency, while a union is an organization formed by workers themselves.
ww.A company's marketing team that plans ad: A marketing team is a department inside a company that plans advertising, which is unrelated to workers' collective bargaining.
ww.A type of bank that lends only to member: A credit union lends to members, but a labor union is not a bank; it represents workers in negotiations with employers.

rw: Employer matching means the company adds money to the employee's 401(k) based on the employee's contribution, often up to a stated percentage of pay.

ww.The employer deletes the account when pa: The employer does not delete the account; a match is extra money added when the employee contributes, not a penalty for low pay.
ww.The employer pays the employee's taxes f: Employer matching contributions go into the retirement account; they do not mean the employer pays the employee's yearly taxes.
ww.The employer takes money from savings to: The match is added to the employee's retirement account by the employer, not taken from savings to cover the employer's bills.

rw: Percent increase = ($16 - $14) / $14 = $2 / $14 = about 14.3%, using the original wage as the base.

ww.About 2.0%: A 2% answer mistakes the $2 dollar raise for a percentage; the percent increase must be measured against the old wage.
ww.About 20.0%: 20% would need a raise of $2.80 on $14, which is more than the actual $2 raise.
ww.About 12.5%: 12.5% divides the $2 raise by the new wage of $16, but percent change must use the original wage as the base.

rw: A part-time job has fewer hours than full-time work, often under 30 to 35 hours a week, and may offer fewer benefits.

ww.A job with no pay for the worker at all: A job with no pay is volunteering; part-time work is paid but involves fewer hours than a full-time job.
ww.A job with exactly 60 hours each week of: Sixty hours a week is more than a typical full-time schedule, so it is not part-time work.
ww.A job for only one day a year, like a ho: One day a year would be an occasional job, not part-time work, which involves regular weekly hours.

rw: Net income is business revenue minus business expenses; it is the profit left for the owner before personal considerations.

ww.Taxes paid on the business income that y: Taxes on business income are a cost the owner pays and do not define net income.
ww.All sales before costs, the total money: All sales before costs describes gross revenue, which is higher than net income.
ww.Money borrowed from a bank to run the bu: Borrowed money is a loan to be repaid, not income, and borrowing does not measure what the business earned.

rw: Net income = sales - expenses = $60,000 - $18,000 = $42,000 of business income before personal taxes.

ww.$18,000: $18,000 is the expense total, not what remains after expenses are subtracted from sales.
ww.$60,000: $60,000 is gross sales before expenses; net income subtracts the $18,000 of costs.
ww.$78,000: $78,000 adds expenses to sales, but expenses must be subtracted to find net income.

rw: A good reference is someone who knows your work and can speak honestly about your skills, reliability, and character to an employer.

ww.A friend who does not know you well but: A friend who barely knows you cannot give meaningful details about your work, so employers gain little from their opinion.
ww.A stranger who has never met you or seen: A stranger has no knowledge of your work or character, so cannot serve as a reference to an employer.
ww.A relative who will lie to make you look: A relative who lies would hurt your credibility; employers want honest, informed references, usually from supervisors or teachers.

rw: Job satisfaction is how content and fulfilled a worker feels about the job, influenced by pay, duties, coworkers, and growth.

ww.The number of coworkers on the staff tea: The number of coworkers is a team-size fact and not a measure of how content a worker feels in the job.
ww.The size of the office you work in each: Office size describes the workplace, while job satisfaction measures how fulfilled a worker feels, regardless of space.
ww.The distance to work from your home each: Commute distance is a logistics factor that may influence satisfaction, but it is not what the term itself means.

rw: A 10% cut saves $45 a month ($450 x 0.10), and $45 x 12 months = $540 per year.

ww.$54: $54 is 12% of $450, which does not match the 10% cut or the yearly total.
ww.$450: $450 is the entire monthly grocery bill, not the yearly savings from a 10% cut.
ww.$45: $45 is only the monthly savings; the question asks for the yearly figure, which is 12 times that.

rw: A basic plan may be a need for communication, while a premium unlimited plan with extras goes beyond what is necessary and is a want.

ww.Plans have no cost, so the choice is nev: Phone plans cost money, so choosing one always involves trade-offs between price and features.
ww.Every plan is a want, so none of them ca: Calling every plan a want ignores that basic phone service may be essential for work, school, or safety.
ww.Every plan is a need at any price, since: Not every plan is a need; a premium unlimited plan with extras goes beyond what is essential, so some plan features are wants.

rw: Entertainment spending changes from month to month depending on choices, which makes it a variable expense.

ww.Monthly rent payment: Monthly rent is usually the same amount each month, which makes it a fixed expense.
ww.A fixed car loan payment: A fixed car loan payment is the same amount each month, so it is a fixed expense rather than variable.
ww.Insurance premium bill: Insurance premiums are typically set amounts due on a schedule, so they are fixed rather than variable expenses.

rw: Fixed costs are $900 + $250 + $100 = $1,250, and $1,250 / $2,400 = about 52% of take-home pay.

ww.About 25%: 25% would be about $600; fixed costs total $900 + $250 + $100 = $1,250, which is more than that.
ww.About 100%: 100% would mean fixed costs equal all take-home pay, but they total $1,250 out of $2,400.
ww.About 12%: 12% would be about $288, far below the $1,250 total of fixed monthly costs.

rw: Comparing unit prices and quality lets a shopper find the best value, not just the lowest sticker price.

ww.Buy the most expensive item that you can: The most expensive item is not necessarily the best; a smart shopper looks for value rather than the highest price.
ww.Buy without checking the price or the qu: Buying without checking prices or quality risks overpaying and getting poor items, which is the opposite of bargain hunting.
ww.Buy the cheapest item always, whatever i: Always buying the cheapest item can backfire if it breaks or doesn't do the job, so quality and use matter too.

rw: Convenience purchases, such as ready-made meals or delivery, often charge a premium for saving the buyer's time or effort.

ww.Always better value than anything else: Convenience items often cost more than comparable ones, so they are not always better value than other options.
ww.Always lower than all other options: Convenience items such as pre-cut food or delivery frequently cost more than alternatives, so they are not always cheaper.
ww.Free of any fees or extra charges at all: Convenience purchases often carry delivery or service fees and higher markups, so they are not free of extra charges.

rw: Yearly cost = $4.50 x 250 workdays = $1,125, which shows how small daily purchases add up over time.

ww.$450: $450 equals only 100 days of $4.50 coffee, far fewer than the 250 workdays in the problem.
ww.$11,250: $11,250 is ten times the correct total; $4.50 x 250 equals $1,125.
ww.$112: $112 corresponds to about 25 days of coffee, not 250 workdays, so it is far too low.

rw: A trade-off means giving up one thing to get another, such as skipping a new game to afford shoes, because resources are limited.

ww.Returning all items that you bought last: Returning items bought last month is a refund choice, not a trade-off, which is about choosing between alternatives.
ww.Buying everything at once on one shoppin: Buying everything at once ignores limited money; a trade-off arises exactly because you cannot afford every item.
ww.Trading with friends only, swapping good: A trade-off is not limited to swapping goods with friends; it is any choice that gives up one option for another.

rw: Tracking your balance and setting low-balance alerts helps you avoid spending more than you have, preventing overdraft fees.

ww.Ignore your balance and spend all that y: Ignoring your balance and spending freely is the quickest way to trigger overdraft fees when payments exceed your funds.
ww.Close your bank account and keep cash at: Closing your account and holding cash gives up banking services and safety, and does not teach balance management.
ww.Write checks without checking your balan: Writing checks without checking the balance risks overdrafts and fees, since checks can bounce when funds are short.

rw: Spending is $80 + $60 + $70 = $210, so the budget remaining is $250 - $210 = $40.

ww.$210: $210 is the total spent ($80 + $60 + $70), not the amount left over from the $250 budget.
ww.$0: Zero would mean all $250 was spent, but she spent only $210 of the budget.
ww.$140: $140 would be left only if she had spent $110; her three purchases total $210.

rw: A loyalty program rewards repeat shoppers with points, discounts, or special offers to keep them buying from the store.

ww.A return penalty charged by the store: A return penalty is a store policy fee, whereas a loyalty program gives rewards to repeat customers.
ww.A fee to enter a store and look around: Stores don't charge people to enter; loyalty programs offer perks to encourage customers to come back.
ww.A tax on frequent buyers added at the ti: Loyalty programs reward frequent buyers; they do not tax them at the register.

rw: Prices for similar coverage vary by insurer, so comparing quotes can help you find the same protection for less money.

ww.All quotes are always identical in price: Quotes are not identical, because insurers weigh risk differently, which is the very reason comparing them is worthwhile.
ww.Quotes are illegal in most of the states: Insurance quotes are legal and free to request, and shopping around is a standard consumer practice.
ww.Quotes eliminate all risk for the buyer: A quote is just a price estimate; it cannot eliminate risk, which is why insurance is bought separately.

rt: Yes, if she wants the item, since she pays $40 instead of $46
rw: If she wants the item, buying it brings her total to $50, and after the $10 coupon she pays $40 instead of $46.

ww.Yes always, because coupons are free mon: Coupons are not free money; spending on an item you do not need can cancel the savings from the discount.
ww.Yes, because she saves $50 on the whole: The coupon saves $10, not $50; $50 is the minimum purchase needed to qualify, not the savings.
ww.No, because coupons never work in any st: Coupons do work when their conditions are met, including at stores she visits, so saying they never work is false.

rw: Shopping with a budget means setting a spending limit beforehand and sticking to it so you spend on priorities, not impulses.

ww.Avoid looking at prices while you shop i: Avoiding prices makes it hard to stay within a budget, because you cannot compare costs to the limit you set.
ww.Spend all your money on the first things: Spending all your money on the first things you see ignores budgeting and leaves nothing for other needs.
ww.Buy whatever looks nice to you at the ti: Buying whatever looks nice is impulse shopping, which tends to lead to overspending.

rw: An installment plan splits the price of a purchase into several scheduled payments, often with interest or fees added.

ww.Receiving a gift from a friend on a spec: A gift is given freely and is not paid for, whereas an installment plan involves scheduled payments for a purchase.
ww.Paying everything at once, in a single l: Paying everything at once is a lump sum purchase, which is the opposite of an installment plan.
ww.Not paying at all for the goods that you: Taking goods without paying is theft, whereas installment plans require full payment in scheduled amounts.

rw: Deposits total $50 x 36 = $1,800; adding about $55 of compound interest at 3% gives roughly $1,855 after 3 years.

ww.About $2,500: $2,500 is far above what $1,800 in deposits plus a few dozen dollars of interest could reach at 3%.
ww.About $1,000: $1,000 is below even the $1,800 she deposits, so it can't be the total after three years of saving.
ww.$1,800 exactly: Deposits alone total $1,800, and interest at 3% adds some more, so the total is slightly above $1,800 and not exactly equal.

rw: Automatic transfers save consistently without needing willpower each month, so saving happens before you can spend the money.

ww.It removes the need for any bank account: Automatic transfers still use bank accounts; they move money between your own accounts without manual effort.
ww.It spends your savings before you can us: Transfers move money into savings, which preserves it for later; they do not spend savings.
ww.It increases fees on your savings accoun: An automatic transfer does not raise account fees; many savings accounts have no fees to begin with.

rw: APY stands for annual percentage yield, the real yearly return on savings after compounding is included, useful for comparing accounts.

ww.Average payment year: APY is not about average payments; it measures the interest earned on a deposit over a year.
ww.Annual payment yield: APY does not stand for a payment yield; it is a savings measure that includes compounding.
ww.Applied profit per year: APY is a standard banking term for annual percentage yield, not profit applied per year.

rw: A savings or checking account offers easy access, insured safety, and no market risk for money you may need within days.

ww.A single volatile stock held in a broker: A volatile stock can lose value quickly, so it is a poor place for money you may need within days.
ww.A 5-year CD with early withdrawal penalt: A 5-year CD charges a penalty for early withdrawal, so it is a poor fit for money needed soon.
ww.A long-term retirement fund of stocks an: Retirement funds are meant for long-term growth and carry market risk and withdrawal limits, which does not suit short-term needs.

rw: Setting a savings priority means deciding which goals matter most, such as an emergency fund, and funding them first.

ww.Save for everything equally with no plan: Saving for everything equally with no plan ignores that some goals matter more and deserve funding first.
ww.Never save anything toward any goal in l: Never saving toward any goal is the opposite of setting priorities, since priorities guide where saved money goes.
ww.Spend first, save later with whatever is: Spending first and saving what is left usually means little gets saved, whereas priorities direct savings before spending.

rw: Months of expenses saved = $3,000 / $1,500 = 2 months, which is below the 3 to 6 months often recommended.

ww.0.5 months: 0.5 months comes from flipping the division ($1,500 / $3,000); the savings are larger than one month of expenses.
ww.6 months: Six months would need $9,000 in savings ($1,500 x 6), but she has only $3,000.
ww.1 month: One month would need only $1,500 in savings, but she has $3,000, which covers two months.

rw: A savings bond is a government debt security bought at a set value that earns interest over time and is repaid at maturity.

ww.A checking account that you use to pay b: A checking account is a deposit account for paying bills, and a savings bond is a government security that earns interest.
ww.A credit card that lets you borrow money: A credit card lets you borrow up to a limit, whereas a savings bond is a loan you make to the government.
ww.A share of a company that is owned by th: A share of a company is stock, which represents ownership, while a savings bond is a government loan.

rw: Keeping savings in a separate account reduces the temptation to spend it and makes it easier to reach your goals.

ww.It removes interest from your account: Savings accounts usually pay interest, so separate accounts don't remove interest; many checking accounts pay little or none.
ww.It prevents deposits from a paycheck: A separate account does not stop paycheck deposits; you can direct part of your pay straight into it.
ww.It increases fees on your own account: Separate accounts do not raise fees; many savings accounts have no fees if you meet minimum balance rules.

rw: With a longer horizon, investments have more time to recover from market dips, so savers can accept more risk for goals far away.

ww.Banks guarantee all returns on long-term: Banks do not guarantee stock returns; deposit insurance covers bank accounts, not market investments.
ww.Risk disappears over time for long-term: Risk does not vanish over time; it only becomes easier to ride out because there is more time to recover.
ww.Investments cannot lose value over a lon: Investments can lose value over any time period, even a long one, though long-term results have usually trended upward.

rw: An emergency fund belongs in a liquid, safe account such as savings so cash is available immediately and not at risk of loss.

ww.Cash buried in a yard in a metal tin box: Cash buried in a tin earns nothing and could be lost, stolen, or destroyed, so it is unsafe for an emergency fund.
ww.A speculative stock bought on a tip: A speculative stock can fall sharply just when you need money, so it is unsuitable for an emergency fund.
ww.A long-term locked CD with penalties: A locked CD charges penalties for early withdrawal, which defeats the purpose of quick access in an emergency.

rw: Saving emphasizes safety and easy access, while investing aims for higher growth but carries the risk of loss.

ww.Investing is for spending only, while sa: This reverses the idea: investing is meant for growth, while saving is for safety and short-term access.
ww.Saving has more risk than investing alwa: Insured bank savings are generally lower risk than investing, so claiming saving always has more risk is incorrect.
ww.They mean the same thing, as both put mo: Saving and investing differ in risk and return; investing buys assets like stocks that may lose value, unlike insured deposits.

rw: Interest = principal x rate = $4,000 x 0.025 = $100 for one year.

ww.$10: $10 would come from a rate of only 0.25%, which is too low; 2.5% of $4,000 is more.
ww.$25: $25 would be about 0.625% of $4,000; the correct 2.5% rate yields four times that.
ww.$1,000: $1,000 is 25% of $4,000, ten times the stated rate of 2.5%.

rw: Dividend yield = annual dividend / price = $2 / $50 = 0.04, or 4%, the annual income return on the share price.

ww.25%: 25% is the price divided by the dividend inverted; yield must divide the dividend by the price.
ww.10%: 10% would need a $5 dividend on a $50 stock; a $2 dividend gives a much lower yield.
ww.2%: Two percent mistakes the $2 dividend for a percentage; dividing by the $50 price gives 4%.

rw: Asset allocation spreads your money among different asset classes such as stocks, bonds, and cash to balance risk and return.

ww.Paying a broker fee for each trade that: Paying broker fees is a cost of trading, not an allocation strategy for spreading money across asset types.
ww.Buying one stock only, which gives the b: Buying one stock only is concentration, the opposite of allocating across different types of investments.
ww.Selling everything you own and holding o: Selling everything for cash abandons investing altogether rather than allocating across several asset classes.

rw: Stocks have historically delivered the highest long-term returns among common assets, but with more ups and downs and risk of loss.

ww.Savings: Savings accounts are safe and liquid but offer low returns, so they lack high long-term growth potential.
ww.Cash: Cash holds its value in the short term but loses purchasing power to inflation and offers little growth.
ww.T-bills: T-bills are very safe government securities with low returns, not high-growth, high-risk investments.

rw: A 3-for-1 split triples the shares and divides the price by 3, so $120 / 3 = $40 per share, with the total value unchanged.

ww.$120: A split does not change the stock price in the way this implies; with 3-for-1, the price falls to a third, not stays at $120.
ww.$30: $30 would result from dividing by four; a 3-for-1 split divides the price by 3, giving $40.
ww.$360: $360 multiplies the price by 3, but a stock split divides the price while increasing the number of shares.

rw: Index funds hold many stocks at once and charge low fees, which gives broad diversification and keeps more of the return for investors.

ww.They guarantee profits for every single: No investment guarantees profits for every investor, and index funds lose value when the market falls.
ww.They are exempt from market risk altoget: Index funds still carry market risk because they track the market; diversification reduces risk but does not erase market-wide declines.
ww.They never change in value over the long: Index fund values rise and fall with the market, so they change in value over time.

rw: Liquidity is how quickly and easily an asset can be turned into cash without a big loss in value; savings are very liquid, real estate is not.

ww.How much water a company uses to make it: Water use by a company is an operations matter and has nothing to do with how easily an asset converts to cash.
ww.How much profit a company makes from its: Company profit measures earnings, while liquidity describes how easily an asset can be sold for cash.
ww.How many shareholders a firm has, found: The number of shareholders is a fact about ownership, whereas liquidity describes how easily an asset can be sold.

rw: Past performance does not guarantee future results, so buying only because of last month's gain may mean buying right before a drop.

ww.It guarantees dividends for every stock: A recent price rise does not guarantee dividends; many stocks that rise pay none at all.
ww.Past gains always repeat, so a rising st: Past gains do not repeat on command, and assuming a rising stock keeps rising is a common cause of buying at the top.
ww.It removes all risk from the investments: No recent gain removes risk; any stock can fall, and chasing recent winners often adds risk.

rw: The statement balance is the total owed at the end of the billing cycle, and paying it in full by the due date avoids interest.

ww.The minimum payment that you must make e: The minimum payment is the smallest amount due, while the statement balance is the full amount owed at the cycle end.
ww.The rewards earned on the card over the: Rewards earned are tracked separately, while the statement balance is the amount owed on the account.
ww.The credit limit that is set on the card: The credit limit is the maximum you can borrow, whereas the statement balance is what you actually owe.

rw: Paying the full $500 statement balance by the due date uses the grace period, so no interest is charged on those purchases.

ww.$18: $18 mistakes the 18% rate for dollars; with the full balance paid on time, no interest is owed.
ww.$7.50: $7.50 would be about one month of interest ($500 x 0.015), but none is charged when the balance is paid in full by the due date.
ww.$90: $90 is a full year of interest at 18% ($500 x 0.18), which applies only if the balance is carried for a year.

rw: Minimum payments cover mostly interest, so the balance shrinks slowly and you pay much more interest over time.

ww.Your limit rises each month: Paying only the minimum does not raise your limit; limits are changed by the issuer based on your credit profile.
ww.You pay no interest at all ever: Unpaid balances accrue interest, so paying only the minimum still costs interest every month.
ww.The debt disappears in a year or so: Minimum payments are small, so debt lasts for years rather than disappearing in a year or so.

rw: Simple interest = principal x rate x time = $2,000 x 0.08 x 2 = $320 in total interest over two years.

ww.$800: $800 would be four years of interest at 8% ($2,000 x 0.08 x 5); the loan runs only 2 years.
ww.$160: $160 is one year of interest ($2,000 x 0.08); the loan lasts two years, so double it.
ww.$3,200: $3,200 is far too high; it equals 80% per year of the principal, not 8%.

rw: A fixed-rate loan keeps the same interest rate for the whole term, so payments are predictable.

ww.A loan with no interest to pay at all: A fixed-rate loan still charges interest; it simply keeps the rate constant over the life of the loan.
ww.A loan that has no payments to make at a: Every loan has payments, and a fixed-rate loan has regular, predictable payments through its term.
ww.A loan whose rate changes with the marke: A loan whose rate changes with the market is a variable-rate loan, the opposite of fixed.

rw: A variable-rate loan's interest rate can rise or fall over time, usually following a benchmark rate, so payments can change.

ww.A loan with the same rate for its whole: A loan with the same rate for its whole life is a fixed-rate loan, not a variable-rate loan.
ww.A loan paid in one single payment on the: Loans paid in one payment are bullet or balloon loans; variable refers to the interest rate, not payment timing.
ww.A loan that has no rate of interest at a: Variable-rate loans charge interest, though the rate changes; no loan of this type is interest-free.

rw: If the benchmark rate rises, the interest rate rises, so monthly payments on a variable-rate loan can increase.

ww.Payments never change in any month: Payments on a variable-rate loan can change from month to month, so they do not stay the same in every month.
ww.The loan has no end date and no limit: Variable-rate loans still have a term and rate caps, so they do not run forever or without limits.
ww.Interest is waived for the borrower: The borrower still pays interest on variable-rate loans; only the rate changes, not whether it is owed.

rw: Collateral is property, like a car or house, pledged to secure a loan that the lender can claim if the borrower defaults.

ww.The interest rate on the loan itself: The interest rate is the cost of borrowing, whereas collateral is property that backs the loan.
ww.A credit report on the borrower: A credit report is a record of the borrower's credit history, while collateral is an asset the lender can claim.
ww.A late fee a lender adds on top: A late fee is a penalty for missed payments, whereas collateral is an asset used as security for repayment.
